chapters.title: Chapter 1: Autoregressive Language Models and Sequence Likelihoods
chapters.description: Introduces autoregressive language models used as policies: their probabilistic formulation, how sequence likelihoods are computed from token-level conditionals, and practical sampling/decoding methods.
subtopics: Autoregressive factorization: p(y|x) = ∏_t p(y_t | x, y_<t)
Tokenization and vocabulary considerations
Softmax output, logits, and log-probabilities
Sequence log-likelihood and per-token log-probabilities
Length effects and length normalization of likelihoods
Sampling/decoding methods: greedy, temperature, top-k, nucleus (top-p)
Perplexity and likelihood-based evaluation
Inference vs training engines and precision differences

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Probability, Expectations, and Importance Sampling
chapters.description: Covers core probability concepts and the theory of importance sampling (IS), which underlies off-policy corrections and likelihood-ratio estimators in RL.
subtopics: Expectation, change of measure, and unbiased estimation
Importance sampling identity and IS estimators
Self-normalized importance sampling
Variance of IS estimators and factors affecting it
Effective sample size and diagnostics for IS
Practical remedies: clipping/truncation and weight normalization

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reinforcement Learning Formulation for Sequence Generation
chapters.description: Frames language generation as an RL problem: policies as LMs, trajectories as sequences, reward assignment, and the episodic setup used in RL for LMs (including RLHF-style settings).
subtopics: MDP / episodic setup for generation tasks
Policy as a conditional language model
Trajectories: queries (contexts) and generated responses
Reward design for sequences and scalar episodic rewards
Return, discounting (if used), and terminal rewards
RLHF overview: preference models, human feedback, and verifier scorers
Batch rollouts and dataset of query–response–reward tuples

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Policy Gradient Methods and the Log-likelihood Trick
chapters.description: Derives policy gradient estimators (score-function/REINFORCE), shows how gradients of expected reward reduce to log-probability gradients, and introduces baselines to reduce variance.
subtopics: Objective: maximize expected reward under policy
Score-function gradient identity (∇θ Eπ[f] = Eπ[f ∇θ log π])
REINFORCE algorithm and Monte Carlo gradient estimates
Use of baselines and value functions to reduce variance
Per-step (per-token) versus per-trajectory gradient formulations
Practical computation of ∇θ log π(y|x) for autoregressive models

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Clipped Surrogate Objectives
chapters.description: Presents PPO's surrogate objective, the importance ratio concept in PPO, clipping mechanisms and KL-regularization, and practical issues when applying PPO to language models.
subtopics: PPO surrogate objective and intuition
Importance ratio r(θ) = π_θ(a)/π_θ_old(a) and its role
Clipped objective: min(r(θ)A, clip(r(θ),1-ε,1+ε)A)
Trust-region motivation and KL penalty alternatives
Per-action (token-level) vs per-episode (sequence-level) implementations
Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) and advantage inputs
Mini-batching, epoch updates, and off-policy considerations in PPO

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Off-policy Learning, Per-decision Importance Sampling, and Truncation
chapters.description: Explores off-policy RL theory and practical per-decision importance sampling techniques, including how IS is applied at different granularities (trajectory vs step) and the attendant variance challenges.
subtopics: On-policy vs off-policy learning distinctions
Per-trajectory vs per-step (per-decision) importance sampling
Self-normalized and truncated IS estimators
When per-step IS is valid and when it introduces bias/variance
Clipping/truncation of importance weights and consequences
Accumulation of variance over long horizons and long sequences

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Advantage Estimation, Baselines, and Group Normalization
chapters.description: Describes methods for computing advantages for policy updates: learned value baselines, sample-based baselines, and group-based normalization techniques used when value functions are unavailable or impractical.
subtopics: Definition of advantage A = return − baseline
Value function learning and bootstrapping
Monte Carlo baselines and per-batch normalization
Group (within-query) advantage normalization: mean/std standardization
Pros and cons of learned value models vs sample normalization
Impact of advantage scaling on training stability

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Variance Reduction and Stabilization Techniques
chapters.description: Surveys practical techniques to stabilize RL training and reduce estimator variance—essential for large models and long sequences.
subtopics: Baselines and critic networks
Reward scaling and normalization
Entropy regularization and exploration control
Gradient clipping and learning-rate schedules
Trust-region methods (TRPO) and proximal methods (PPO)
Replay strategies and their role in stability
Diagnostics: monitoring importance weights, KL, and clipped fractions

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Architectures and Routing
chapters.description: Explains sparse Mixture-of-Experts models: how experts are routed, the sources of activation volatility, and implications for likelihood computation and distributed training.
subtopics: MoE layer structure: experts and gating/routing networks
Top-k gating, load balancing, and auxiliary losses
Sparse activation: per-token expert selection and efficiency
Routing variability across parameter updates and its effects
Computing likelihoods in MoE: consistency concerns
Memory, communication, and implementation trade-offs

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Gradient Analysis for Sequence Models and Likelihood Ratios
chapters.description: Analyzes gradients for sequence generation objectives, shows how token-level log gradients compose into sequence gradients, and discusses how different weighting schemes affect gradient estimates.
subtopics: Gradient of log-likelihood for a sequence: sum over token gradients
Relationship between per-token weighting and overall sequence gradient
Effect of weighting/importance ratios on gradient magnitudes
Accumulation of noise across long sequences
Practical computation: detaching, stop-gradient semantics, and numerical concerns
Comparing per-step IS weighting vs trajectory-level weighting

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Training Infrastructure and Practical Considerations for Large-scale RL
chapters.description: Covers operational aspects of running RL at large scale with LMs: rollouts, batching, minibatches, partial rollout, recomputation of likelihoods, engine precision, and distributed pipeline issues.
subtopics: Rollout generation pipelines and query sets
Batching, splitting into mini-batches, and epoch-based updates
Partial rollouts and multi-turn episode handling
Inference engines vs training engines: likelihood recomputation and precision
Checkpointing, reproducibility, and deterministic vs non-deterministic ops
Communication and memory bottlenecks in distributed RL

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Numerical Stability, Length Effects, and Normalization Strategies
chapters.description: Focuses on numerical issues that arise in likelihood-based RL: floating-point precision, log-sum-exp tricks, length normalization, and how these choices affect importance weights and clipping.
subtopics: Floating-point precision: fp16/bfloat16 vs fp32 and consequences
Computing log-probabilities safely: log-sum-exp and underflow/overflow
Length normalization of sequence likelihoods and motivations
Scaling and choosing clipping ranges for different likelihood definitions
Diagnostic metrics: magnitude and variance of importance ratios
Practical heuristics to control numerical instability

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Evaluation Metrics, Benchmarks, and Experimental Design
chapters.description: Reviews common evaluation metrics and experimental protocols used to assess RL-trained language models, including sampling-based metrics and benchmark suites referenced in research.
subtopics: Pass@k metrics and sampling-based evaluation for coding/math tasks
Elo ratings and pairwise evaluation methods
Benchmarks for reasoning and coding (e.g., AIME, CodeForces)
Statistical considerations: variance across seeds, significance testing
Ablation studies and hyperparameter sweeps
Reporting training curves: reward, clipped fractions, KL, and wall-clock compute

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Mathematical Tools and Identities for Analysis
chapters.description: Collects mathematical tools commonly used in the analysis of RL algorithms and likelihood-based objectives to facilitate formal derivations and variance analyses.
subtopics: Logarithms and exponentials: properties and manipulations
Taylor expansions for small perturbations
Jensen's and other inequalities used in expectations
Transformations between sums and expectations
Back-of-the-envelope variance approximations
Interpreting gradients and sensitivity via linearization
